Learning Objectives
Identify the most common entrapment neuropathies of the foot and ankle.
Obtain an appropriate patient history and perform an appropriate physical examination in
patients with potential entrapment neuropathy.
Recognize the sensory and motor deficits associated with each entrapment neuropathy.
Review the common treatment options and outcomes for patients with nerve entrapment of
the foot and ankle.

General information
Pathologic conditions of the central and peripheral nervous systems may cause symptomatic
dysfunction of the foot and ankle.
Central nervous system pathology results in upper motor neuron findings (spasticity and
hyperreflexia).
Peripheral nerve lesions result in lower motor neuron findings (weakness, decreased
reflexes, absence of spasticity, and atrophy).
Innervation of the foot and ankle
Sensation to the foot and ankle is supplied by five nerves: tibial, deep peroneal, superficial
peroneal, sural, and saphenous.
Motor innervation is provided by the tibial (intrinsics and posterior leg compartment), deep
peroneal (anterior leg compartment and extensor digitorum brevis [EDB]), and superficial
peroneal (lateral leg compartment) nerves.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Tibial Nerve
The most common compression neuropathy affecting the foot and ankle is tarsal tunnel
syndrome (TTS).
The contents of the tarsal tunnel include the tibialis posterior tendon; flexor digitorum longus
tendon; posterior tibial vein and artery; tibial nerve; flexor hallucis longus tendon; and
posterior tibial artery, nerve, and vein (Figure 1; Resource 1).

Figure 1 Illustration of the medial aspect of the foot shows the tarsal tunnel. (Reproduced
from Wukich DK: Neurologic disorders of the foot and ankle, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 1204-1219.)
The flexor retinaculum (laciniate ligament) bridges the leg fascia proximally and the fascia of
the abductor hallucis distally.
The posterior tibial nerve has three terminal branches: the medial plantar, lateral plantar, and
medial calcaneal nerves.
These three terminal nerves most commonly branch within the tarsal tunnel; however,
branching can occur proximal or distal to the laciniate ligament.
The medial and lateral plantar nerves each travel in their own fibrous tunnel distal to the tarsal
tunnel. Distal TTS describes compression of the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Figure
2).

Figure 2 Coronal view illustration of the hindfoot shows two areas (1, 2) of possible
impingement of the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (ie, Baxter nerve). (Reproduced
from Lareau CR, Sawyer GA, Wang JH, DiGiovanni CW: Plantar and medial heel pain: Diagnosis
and management. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2014;22[6]:372–380.)
Deep Peroneal Nerve
The deep peroneal nerve (DPN) travels with the anterior tibial artery in the interval between
the extensor digitorum longus and the extensor hallucis longus (EHL). Just proximal to the
ankle, the nerve bifurcates into a lateral branch, which innervates the EDB, and a medial
branch, which supplies sensation to the first dorsal web space.
Superficial Peroneal Nerve
The superficial peroneal nerve (SPN) branches from the common peroneal nerve (CPN) at the
level of the fibular neck and proceeds distally in the lateral compartment between the
peroneus brevis and peroneus longus muscles.

This purely sensory nerve becomes superficial by piercing the crural fascia in the distal third
of the leg and, approximately 10 cm above the tip of the distal fibula, branches into the
medial dorsal cutaneous nerve and the intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve (Figure 3).
The intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve provides dorsal sensation to the third, fourth,
and fifth toes.
The medial dorsal cutaneous nerve passes lateral to the EHL and provides sensation to the
medial aspect of the dorsal foot.

Sural Nerve
The sural nerve is a purely sensory nerve that is formed by branches of the peroneal and
tibial nerves.
At the musculotendinous junction of the gastrocnemius muscle, the sural nerve lies at the
midline and then descends distally lateral to the Achilles tendon.
As the nerve progresses distally, it lies posterior to the peroneal tendons and then supplies
branches to the lateral hindfoot. It then proceeds distally and crosses the base of the fifth
metatarsal.
Saphenous Nerve
The saphenous nerve provides sensation to the medial ankle and a portion of the
dorsomedial foot.
The nerve follows the greater saphenous vein and can be injured during anteromedial
arthroscopic portal placement.
Saphenous nerve entrapment is rare in the foot and ankle and usually occurs proximally, at
the medial aspect of the knee.

Anatomy and Biomechanics
TTS is one of the most common entrapment neuropathies of the foot and ankle. At
the level of the popliteal fossa, the tibial nerve, a branch of the sciatic nerve, provides
motor innervation to the muscles of the superficial and deep posterior compartment.
As it travels distally, the tibial nerve approaches the tarsal tunnel. The tarsal tunnel is
a fibro-osseous canal defined by the tibia anteriorly, talus and sustentaculum tali of
the calcaneus laterally, and the flexor retinaculum (or laciniate ligament) medially. The
tibial nerve enters the canal proximally and divides into the medial calcaneal nerve,
medial plantar nerve, and lateral plantar nerve. These terminal branches provide
sensation to the posterior heel and the medial and lateral aspects of the plantar foot;
however, great anatomic variation exists in the branching patterns within the tibial
nerve and the number of branches of the calcaneal nerve.1-3 Compression can occur
along any portion of the tibial nerve or its branches.
The DPN arises from the CPN at the proximal fibula. It travels into the anterior
compartment and gives off motor branches to the muscles in this compartment. In
the middle third of the leg, it travels between the tibialis anterior and EHL. At 3 to 5
cm proximal to the ankle joint, the EHL crosses over the nerve, placing the nerve

9/4/26, 10:16 AM
AAOS | Neurogenic Conditions: Entrapment Neuropathy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000006
7/35

between the EHL and the extensor digitorum longus. The DPN then travels under the
extensor retinaculum and divides into its terminal medial and lateral branches
approximately 1 cm proximal to the ankle joint.4,5 The medial branch supplies
cutaneous sensation in the first web space, whereas the lateral branch provides
motor function to the EDB and the extensor hallucis brevis (EHB). Entrapment
neuropathy of the DPN typically occurs in the anterior ankle and dorsal foot within the
anterior tarsal tunnel, which is bordered by the talonavicular joint capsule posteriorly
and the inferior extensor retinaculum anteriorly.
The SPN provides sensory innervation to the anterolateral leg and motor innervation
to the lateral compartment of the leg. It arises from the CPN at the level of the fibular
neck and runs between the peroneal muscles in the lateral compartment, providing
motor branches to the peroneal longus and brevis. As the nerve travels distally, it
becomes purely sensory. As the SPN reaches the distal third of the leg, approximately
8 to 12.5 cm proximal to the tip of the fibula, it pierces the deep crural fascia and
becomes subcutaneous.6,7 The crural fascia is a common site of entrapment. The SPN
then typically branches into the medial dorsal cutaneous nerve and the intermediate
dorsal cutaneous nerve, which supply sensation to the medial and lateral aspects of
the dorsal foot, respectively. As with the tibial nerve, anatomic variability exists with
regard to the distal course and terminal branching pattern of the SPN.
Saphenous nerve entrapment is not common and typically occurs at the level of the
knee. The saphenous nerve is a purely sensory nerve and runs with the superficial
femoral artery in the thigh. At approximately 10 cm proximal to the medial femoral
condyle of the knee, the saphenous nerve penetrates the subsartorial fascia and
enters the adductor canal. This is the most common site of entrapment. Distal to the
knee, the saphenous nerve travels along the medial tibia with the greater saphenous
vein. The terminal branches arise approximately 15 cm proximal to the ankle and
supply sensation to the anteromedial ankle and foot.
Etiology
Tibial nerve
Various causes of TTS have been described, including soft-tissue and osseous trauma; space-
occupying masses (ganglion cyst, lipoma, neurilemmoma, varicose vein, anomalous muscle

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000006
8/35

belly); biomechanical malalignment of the ankle and foot; and tenosynovitis of the tibialis
posterior, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus tendons.
Iatrogenic injury to the lateral plantar nerve may occur during procedures on the plantar
surface of the hindfoot. The lateral plantar nerve is particularly at risk during retrograde
insertion of an intramedullary nail for ankle and hindfoot arthrodesis and resection of
plantar heel spurs.
DPN
Compression of the DPN in the region of the anterior ankle and the dorsal foot results from
entrapment under the superior and inferior extensor retinacula (Figure 4).
Compression under the inferior extensor retinaculum has been referred to as anterior TTS.
Compression of the nerve can may result from osteophytes (on the tibia and/or talus),
avulsion fractures, an enlarged muscle belly of the EDB, ganglion cysts, synovitis, and tumors.
Traction injuries can occur from ankle sprains (Figure 5).

under the hypertrophied extensor hallucis brevis (proximal circle); at the inferior edge of the
inferomedial extensor retinaculum—the classic anterior tarsal tunnel syndrome (middle
circle); and under the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus at the superior edge of the

McGarvey WC: Peripheral nerve entrapments. Foot Ankle Clin 2004;9[2]:255-269.)
SPN
Compression of the SPN can arise anywhere along its course and usually is posttraumatic
in nature. Iatrogenic injury can occur during open management of distal fibula fractures
and placement of the anterolateral ankle portal for arthroscopy.
The most common site of compression of the SPN is the location at which it exits the deep
crural fascia.
Sural nerve
Sural nerve entrapment may result from fractures of the calcaneus, talus, or fifth
metatarsal. Iatrogenic injury may occur during gastrocnemius recession or open reduction
and internal fixation of fractures involving the calcaneus or the base of the fifth metatarsal.

Etiology
The etiology of entrapment neuropathies of the foot and ankle are varied and, in most
patients, multifactorial. A thorough understanding of the anatomic course of the
peripheral nerve and its variations may be important to localize injury or compression
to the nerve.
In TTS, a specific cause can be identified in 60% to 80% of patients.8 The most
common cause of TTS is trauma to the tibial nerve.9 Direct injury from displaced
fractures of the tibia, talus, or calcaneus, and traction injury from ankle sprains may
result in compression of the tibial nerve within the tarsal tunnel. Surgical procedures,
such as retrograde intramedullary nail fixation and resection of plantar heel spurs,
also may result in injury to the distal branches of the tibial nerve.
Another common cause of tibial nerve entrapment is a space-occupying lesion. These
lesions include ganglion cysts, lipomas, neurofibromas, neurilemmoma, bony
exostoses, and accessory muscles within the tarsal tunnel. Compression also may
arise from vascular varicosities and from local inflammation, synovitis, and fibrosis.
Finally, postural deformities of the ankle (varus/valgus) and foot
(pronation/abduction) may result in direct compression or traction injury to the tibial
nerve.

Entrapment of the DPN typically occurs in its distal course along the anterior ankle
and dorsal foot. In most patients, compression and repetitive mechanical irritation of
the DPN occurs as it travels under the inferior extensor retinaculum; this condition is
commonly called anterior TTS. Other sites of entrapment of the DPN include the EHL
tendon, the EHB muscle belly, dorsal osteophytes, or bony prominences/osteophytes
of the ankle or midfoot joints (tibiotalar joint, talonavicular joint, naviculocuneiform
joints, os intermetatarseum).10 In addition, recurrent ankle sprains resulting in
traction injury to the DPN and tight-fitting shoes or boots and space-occupying lesions
leading to anterior compression of the DPN have been described. Irritation of the DPN
also may result from repetitive ankle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion (eg, in athletes
and dancers) and prolonged sitting on a plantarflexed ankle (eg, while praying).
The most common cause of entrapment of the SPN occurs as the nerve pierces the
deep crural fascia. As the nerve exits the deep fascia, the SPN can be compressed by
fascial edge and the presence of any muscle herniation. As many as 60% of patients
have palpable fascial defects. In addition, traction injury to the SPN result from
inversion injuries to the ankle. Moreover, direct trauma to or compression of the SPN
may occur in patients with a fibular fracture or space-occupying lesions (eg, ganglion
cyst, tumor). Iatrogenic injury to the nerve may occur during surgery, including the
lateral approach to the fibula and the dorsomedial approach to the hallux, as well as
during creation of the anterolateral ankle arthroscopy portal.
Entrapment of the sural nerve may result from injury, irritation, or inflammation of
the nerve. Direct lateral ankle or foot trauma or traction from inversion trauma to the
ankle are common precipitating factors. Iatrogenic injury from surgical procedures
(eg, open reduction and internal fixation of a calcaneal fracture, gastrocnemius
recession) has been observed.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Tibial Nerve
Pain associated with TTS may be quite vague but often is characterized as burning with
paresthesias.

14/35

Symptoms usually are aggravated by activities, such as walking, prolonged standing, and
running, and patients often report pain that radiates proximally and distally.
Deep Peroneal Nerve
Patients report a burning pain on the dorsum of the foot with paresthesias in the first dorsal
web space. This pain usually is exacerbated by activities and relieved with rest.
Nocturnal pain is common because the plantarflexed foot places the nerve on stretch. Shoes
with a high heel may induce this plantarflexed posture, reproducing symptoms. Tight-fitting
shoes or boots may cause external compression.
Superficial Peroneal Nerve
Compression of the SPN typically causes anterolateral distal leg and ankle pain and dorsal foot
pain.
The pain occurs in a distribution similar to the L5 distribution and may be associated with
sensory dysfunction in this distribution. The most common site of compression is the location
at which the nerve pierces the leg fascia (deep crural fascia) and becomes superficial.
Sural Nerve
Patients typically report lateral foot and ankle pain that radiates proximally and associated
numbness in that distribution.

Patient History
In all patients in whom nerve entrapment is suspected, a comprehensive history and
physical examination is imperative because most diagnoses are made without any
additional information. However, all patients should be concurrently evaluated for
alternative causes of nerve pain. These include lower back pain and radiculopathy,
diabetes mellitus, peripheral vascular disease, inflammatory conditions, thyroid
dysfunction, Lyme disease, alcoholism, vitamin deficiencies, and metabolic disorders.
Nerve pathology proximal to the lower leg should be evaluated because it may result in
double crush syndrome.

Patients with TTS may report a history of trauma or injury to the foot or ankle that
preceded the onset of pain. The pain may be diffuse but typically is located directly over
the tarsal tunnel with radiation to the plantar foot. Pain is characterized as burning,
shooting, electrical, tingling, or numbness along the medial ankle and/or plantar foot.
The pain typically radiates distally; however, some patients experience proximal
radiation of the pain along the medial aspect of the leg (Valleix phenomenon). Prolonged
standing and increased physical activity exacerbate symptoms, whereas rest provides
relief; however, pain that persists after rest and pain in bed at night also have been
reported.
Entrapment of the DPN typically will manifest as dorsal foot pain radiating to the first
web space. Symptoms associated with external compression on the anterior ankle and
dorsal foot (eg, from tight-fitting shoes, tight lacing, boots, sitting up with the anterior
ankle/foot under a rigid support, repetitive kicking from soccer) and with increased
plantar flexion of the foot (eg, when wearing high heels) are common.11,12 Patients also
may report night pain with the foot is resting in plantar flexion, which results in traction
to the DPN.
Many patients with SPN entrapment report a history of direct trauma (eg, ankle sprain,
fracture, contusion from sports) or surgical treatment (eg, open reduction and internal
fixation, ankle arthroscopy). Pain and paresthesia are noted along the distal course of
the SPN along the anterolateral leg and ankle and dorsal foot. Physical activities involving
plantar flexion and inversion of the ankle (eg, running, squatting) exacerbate pain.
Nocturnal pain is not common in patients with SPN entrapment.
Entrapment of the sural nerve results in irritation or inflammation along the course of
the nerve. A history of ankle sprains or lower extremity surgery to the posterior calf or
lateral ankle/foot is common. Direct pressure on the nerve from footwear may aggravate
symptoms.
Physical Examination
Tibial Nerve

AAOS | Neurogenic Conditions: Entrapment Neuropathy
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000006
16/35

Objective physical findings often are lacking, except for a positive nerve percussion sign (Tinel
sign) along the distribution of the tibial nerve.
Motor and sensory examinations usually are normal.
Pressures within the tarsal tunnel are increased with ankle dorsiflexion and foot eversion, and
this positioning may reproduce the symptoms of TTS.
Electrodiagnostic studies are accurate in diagnosing TTS in 80% to 90% of patients.
Sensory nerve conduction velocity (NCV) study results are more likely to be abnormal than
motor NCV study results.
Electrodiagnostic studies are useful in diagnosing more proximal causes of nerve
compression (eg, radiculopathy).
The value of needle electromyography is a subject of debate.
Deep Peroneal Nerve
Positive findings include weakness and/or atrophy of the EDB, reduced sensation in the first
dorsal web space, and a positive Tinel sign over the area of compression.
Superficial Peroneal Nerve
Motor findings are normal unless compression occurs proximally.
Pain can be reproduced via plantar flexion and inversion and with direct compression of the
nerve. The Tinel sign is useful for determining the site of compression.
Sensory NCV studies may be prolonged; however, electrodiagnostic testing is most useful for
excluding a more proximal cause of nerve compression.
Sural Nerve
A positive percussion test typically reproduces paresthesias in the lateral foot.
NCV studies may demonstrate an increase in distal latency or a decrease in the nerve action
potential, but they rarely are helpful.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Tibial Nerve
Weight-bearing radiographs are useful for assessing the osseous architecture. SEND FEEDBACK

Deep Peroneal Nerve
Radiographs of the ankle and foot should be obtained to assess for osteophytes of the distal
tibia, dorsal talus, or dorsal talonavicular joint.
Superficial Peroneal Nerve
Radiographs help evaluate for osseous impingement (exostosis or spurs); however, the
diagnosis usually is made based on clinical examination.
Sural Nerve
Radiographs are useful for excluding fractures and exostosis.
Computed Tomography
Tibial Nerve
CT may aid in assessment of osseous anatomy in patients with osseous impingement
(posteromedial process fractures of the talus).
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Tibial Nerve
MRI may be useful to evaluate for space-occupying masses and tenosynovitis (Figure 6).

Superficial Peroneal Nerve

Sural Nerve
MRI is beneficial for diagnosing soft-tissue lesions, such as ganglion cysts, which may cause
compression.
Other Studies

Electrodiagnostic studies may show a delay in latency and denervation of the EDB; however,
normal results are common.
Differential Diagnosis
Superficial Peroneal Nerve
The differential diagnosis includes lateral ankle sprains that do not heal, chronic compartment
syndrome, fascial defects, muscle herniations, and proximal nerve entrapment.
Sural Nerve
A positive percussion test typically reproduces paresthesias in the lateral foot.
The differential diagnosis includes lumbosacral radiculopathy, popliteal artery entrapment,
disorders of the Achilles tendon, and chronic pain from lateral ankle sprains.
NCV studies may demonstrate an increase in distal latency or a decrease in the nerve action
potential, but they rarely are helpful.

Differential Diagnosis
Clinical examination of all patients in whom entrapment neuropathy of the foot and
ankle is suspected begins with assessment of alignment. With the patient standing,
hindfoot alignment (varus/valgus) and any posttraumatic deformities should be
identified. Observing the patient walk may reveal dynamic factors resulting in instability
and malalignment that may cause nerve entrapment. In addition, provocative tests may
be performed to confirm suspected nerve entrapment.
Range of motion testing of the ankle, hindfoot, midfoot, and forefoot joints, as well as
assessment of muscle bulk and strength, should be performed and compared with the
contralateral side. Muscle atrophy and contractures may be present in patients with
chronic nerve entrapment. In addition, sensation should be formally assessed via light
touch and two-point discrimination.

Areas of pain should be thoroughly examined and evaluated. In patients in whom nerve
entrapment is suspected, the entire length of the nerve of interest should be palpated
and percussed to localize areas of irritation and discomfort (Tinel sign). Patients typically
will feel a reproduction of the painful paresthesia. For the SPN, specific provocative tests
have been described.13 With the ankle dorsiflexed and everted against resistance, the
site of nerve impingement is palpated. This is repeated with the ankle plantarflexed and
inverted.
The symptoms associated with SPN entrapment may be similar to those of lumbar (L5)
radiculopathy. In both situations, patients may present with weakness of the foot
dorsiflexors and the toe extensors and sensory changes in similar distributions;
however, patients with peroneal entrapment typically have weakness with eversion
compared with weakness in inversion in patients with lumbar pathology. In addition,
changes in reflexes and pain with provocative testing (eg, straight leg raise) noted in
patients with lumbar radiculopathy may help distinguish lumbar radiculopathy from SPN
entrapment.
Although a diagnosis of a nerve entrapment of the foot and ankle typically is made
based on the clinical history and physical examination findings, imaging studies may
provide additional information useful in determining the etiology of symptoms. Plain
weight-bearing radiographs allow for the identification of fractures and provide details
on the osseous architecture of the foot and ankle. Osteophytes, such as those
associated with entrapment of the DPN, can be visualized on the distal tibia or dorsal
midfoot joints. CT may provide higher resolution of bony details, which may be
important in posttraumatic patients; however, such imaging often is not necessary. MRI
may aid in identifying space-occupying lesions and associated soft-tissue injuries.
Electrodiagnostic studies, including electromyography and nerve conduction studies,
may provide insight into the function of the nerves of the foot and ankle and should be
correlated with the clinical history and physical examination findings. Nerves in the
proximal leg also should be included to evaluate for more proximal nerve pathologies
that may represent radiculopathy or double crush syndrome. In TTS, sensory NCV
studies appear to be the most accurate, with a sensitivity of approximately 90%;14
however, controversy exists with regard to how to perform the studies and how to

21/35

interpret the results. Therefore, although a positive test may help confirm suspected
nerve entrapment, a normal test does not necessarily rule out the diagnosis.13
Injections of local anesthetic (lidocaine) in the area of suspected entrapment may be
useful for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. Differential injections also may be
performed to distinguish nerve entrapment from intra-articular pathology.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Tibial nerve
NSAIDs, cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors, local corticosteroid injections, and immobilization are
used to decrease inflammation in the tarsal tunnel.
Immobilization in a removable boot or cast is recommended after steroid injections to
prevent iatrogenic rupture of the tibialis posterior tendon.
Off-the-shelf or custom orthoses may be beneficial if mechanical malalignment is present.
DPN
Reducing pressure over the nerve by avoiding tight-fitting shoes and high heels is
recommended.
If patients have chronic edema, a diuretic may be useful.
Corticosteroid and local anesthetic injections help confirm the diagnosis and direct
management. If the patient does not experience relief during the initial effect of the local
anesthesia, the diagnosis should be reassessed.
SPN
Nonsurgical treatment measures include injections of local anesthetic agents and steroids
and orthoses to prevent inversion of the ankle and foot.
Patients may undergo physical therapy to strengthen the muscles of the foot and ankle and
to desensitize the nerve.
Sural nerve
Accommodative footwear may relieve pressure on the sural nerve.
Injections of local anesthetic agents and corticosteroids may be diagnostic and therapeutic.

Nonsurgical Management
Nonsurgical management of nerve entrapments of the foot and ankle focuses on
medication management and structural support. Although no consensus exists with
regard to the most effective cocktail for management, medications used include NSAIDs,
vitamin B1/B6/B12, antiseizure medications (eg, pregabalin, gabapentin),
antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, duloxetine), and selective serotonin
reuptake inhibitors (eg, sertraline). Topical medications (diclofenac, capsaicin, lidocaine
patches) and compounding creams also may be beneficial.
In patients with postural deformities of the hindfoot or ankle instability, custom orthotics
and bracing may help improve lower extremity alignment and subsequently offload the
compression or limit traction to the affected nerve. In addition, a short course of
immobilization with the use of a controlled ankle motion walker, short leg cast, or night
splint may help reduce inflammation and pain. In addition, physical therapy may help
strengthen muscles and correct potential dynamic causes of nerve entrapment.
Injections of local anesthetic (lidocaine) and corticosteroids in the area of suspected
entrapment may be useful for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. In patients who do
not experience any transient relief from an injection, alternative diagnoses should be
explored.
Surgical Management
Indications
Tibial nerve
Patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails are candidates for surgical decompression.
DPN
If nonsurgical management fails, then neurolysis is indicated.
SPN
If nerve entrapment does not respond to nonsurgical measures, then neurolysis is indicated.
Sural nerve

Techniques/Procedures
Tibial nerve
The tibial nerve should be identified proximal to the tarsal tunnel and decompressed,
including releasing the flexor retinaculum.
The medial plantar, lateral plantar, and medial calcaneal nerves should be identified and
decompressed.
Distal tarsal tunnel release is indicated in patients with associated chronic plantarmedial heel
pain.
The first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Baxter nerve, or nerve to the abductor digiti
minimi quinti) should be decompressed by releasing the deep fascia of the abductor hallucis.
DPN
Decompression of the nerve is begun just proximal to the superior extensor retinaculum and
extends to the base of the first and second tarsometatarsal joint.
Osteophytes should be resected, and hypertrophied muscles can be debulked.
Approximately 80% of patients have a satisfactory result.
SPN
If nerve entrapment does not respond to nonsurgical measures, then neurolysis is indicated.
Surgical decompression should begin at the level at which the nerve exits the fascia.
The area of compression usually can be isolated preoperatively by using the Tinel sign;
neurolysis must proceed distal to the site of compression.
If associated muscle herniation or chronic compartment syndrome is present, then
concurrent fasciotomy is recommended.
Approximately 80% of patients experience clinical improvement; however, patient
satisfaction is not universal.
Sural nerve
If a true posttraumatic neuroma is present, then resection and burying of the proximal
stump is recommended.
Saphenous nerve
If a true neuroma is present, then resection and burying of the proximal stump is
recommended because of its subcutaneous location.

Outcomes
Tibial nerve
The best results after tarsal tunnel release occur in patients with symptoms in the
distribution of the tibial nerve, a positive nerve compression sign, positive electrodiagnostic
studies, and space-occupying masses.
Overall results after tarsal tunnel surgery vary greatly, with successful outcomes in 50% to
90% of patients. The causes of suboptimal results include double crush syndrome,
inadequate release, postoperative hematoma formation, scarring around the nerve, and
improper diagnosis.
Revision tarsal tunnel release is associated with less successful outcomes than primary
release. The best results occur in patients in whom previous decompression of the nerve was
inadequate.
Wrapping the nerve with autologous veins or commercially available nerve wraps may help
prevent scar formation in revision cases.

Outcomes
Surgical treatment is indicated in patients who do not respond to nonsurgical
treatments; however, in patients with a discrete and defined cause of nerve entrapment
that is unlikely to respond to nonsurgical management, surgical treatment may be
considered a first-line treatment option. The most common example of is a space-
occupying lesion. Other examples include rigid bony deformities, prominent hardware,
and instability. In patients without a defined nonneurogenic cause of pain, surgical
treatment should be considered after nonsurgical treatment options have been
exhausted. The site of maximal pain and tenderness should be identified because it will
guide surgical decompression and neurolysis.
Release of the tibial nerve should begin proximal to the tarsal tunnel. The flexor
retinaculum is identified and released from proximal to distal, which decompresses and
reveals the underlying tibial nerve. The nerve is then carefully inspected along its length,
and any areas of compression are identified and released. Each terminal branch of the
tibial nerve is examined and decompressed as necessary. The medial plantar nerve
should be traced, and the fibrous tunnel that it travels in the abductor hallucis should be

Patients who most benefit from tarsal tunnel release are those with a defined cause of
the entrapment. For example, patients with a space-occupying lesion may achieve more
reliable relief of symptoms via removal of the compressive force and decompression of
the nerve; however, in patients with no specific etiology, 25% experience little to no relief
from surgical treatment. Overall, the success rate of tarsal tunnel surgery ranges from
50% to 90%.15-18 Poorer outcomes are associated with inadequate nerve
decompression, postoperative hematoma or scar formation, and increased duration of
symptoms.
Persistent or recurring pain after tarsal tunnel release is a challenge to manage.
Although continued pain may be the result of inadequate release or incorrect diagnosis,
surgical management may result in compressive scar formation or bleeding.
Alternatively, the severity of the initial damage to the nerve may result in intrinsic nerve

management of failed primary tarsal tunnel release include revision neurolysis, revision
neurolysis with nerve wrap to reduce adhesions, nerve transection and burial, and
implantation of peripheral nerve or spinal cord stimulators. Revision tarsal tunnel
surgery (release with or without the addition of nerve wrap) is less successful than
primary surgery, with patient satisfaction rates ranging from 60% to 70%.19-21
Complete surgical release of the DPN extends from the superior extensor retinaculum to
the base of the metatarsals. The area of maximal tenderness should be identified
preoperatively. If the area of compression is at the inferior or superior extensor
retinaculum, as much as 50% of the retinaculum can be released before a formal Z-
lengthening procedure is performed to avoid bowstringing of the extensor tendons. In
addition, areas of dorsal prominence and osteophytes should be localized and removed
to stable borders. Studies have demonstrated satisfactory outcomes in 80% to 90% of
patients with DPN entrapment managed via surgical decompression.22,23 Better results
occur in patients with discrete causes of compression (eg, retinacular entrapment,
impinging osteophytes).
Entrapment of the SPN typically occurs at the deep crural fascia. In most patients, a
localized area exists at which the muscle herniates through the fascia and compresses
the crossing SPN. Rather than repair or close the herniation, the deep crural fascia is
released. The length of the SPN is examined, and any additional sites of compression are
addressed. Satisfactory outcomes have been reported in approximately 75% to 85% of
patients.13,24,25
Surgical management of entrapment of the sural and saphenous nerve involves
exploration and decompression similar to that already described; however, because of
the subcutaneous nature of these nerves, a traumatic or, even, transected branch of the
nerve may be encountered. In such situations, resection and burial of the proximal
stump typically is performed. The transected nerve may be buried in muscle or bone.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
General information
Pathologic conditions of the central and peripheral nervous systems may cause symptomatic
dysfunction of the foot and ankle.
Central nervous system pathology results in upper motor neuron findings (spasticity and
hyperreflexia).
Peripheral nerve lesions result in lower motor neuron findings (weakness, decreased
reflexes, absence of spasticity, atrophy).
Innervation of the foot and ankle
Sensation to the foot and ankle is supplied by five nerves: tibial, deep peroneal, superficial
peroneal, sural, and saphenous.
Motor innervation is provided by the tibial (intrinsics and posterior leg compartment), deep
peroneal (anterior leg compartment and EDB), and superficial peroneal (lateral leg
compartment) nerves.
Etiology
Knee trauma (dislocation)
Lengthening of the sciatic nerve during total hip arthroplasty (CPN is more vulnerable to
lengthening than the tibial nerve)
Total knee arthroplasty in patients with genu valgum
Lumbar radiculopathy
Peripheral neuropathy
Double crush syndrome (ie, diabetes mellitus and lengthening after total hip arthroplasty)

Etiology
Common peroneal neuropathy is the most common mononeuropathy of the lower
extremity and the third most common focal neuropathy overall behind median and
ulnar neuropathies.26,27 The CPN is one of the two major branches of the sciatic nerve
that provides considerable motor and sensory function to the lower leg. After its
branching off from the sciatic nerve in the distal thigh, the CPN travels superficially

and DPN.
The most common cause of CPN is injury or trauma resulting in stretch or compression
of the nerve. The nerve is most vulnerable to injury as it crosses the proximal fibular
neck over the lateral knee. Direct injuries, including proximal fibular fractures and
penetrating trauma, have been described. Injury to the CPN has been reported in as
many as 40% of patients with a knee dislocation.28,29 External compression from a tight
splint or cast, positioning during surgery, and constant leg crossing also may cause
peroneal nerve damage. Traction neurapraxia to the CPN may be seen in lengthening
associated with total hip arthroplasty and in the correction of genu valgum during total
knee arthroplasty.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Ankle-foot orthosis (AFO)
Surgical Management
Achilles tendon or gastrocnemius lengthening for ankle contracture
Posterior tibial tendon transfer through the interosseous membrane (Bridle procedure)
The posterior tibial tendon is split, with half used to substitute for the tibialis anterior and
half used to substitute for the peroneus brevis.
The tendons can be directly sutured to the tibialis anterior and the peroneus brevis (ie,
Pulvertaft weave) or biotenodesis screws can be used.
Recently, a tri-tendon anastomosis has been described that passes the tibialis posterior
through slits in the tibialis anterior and the peroneus longus.
This technique is similar to the classic Bridle procedure, but the transferred tibialis
posterior is not split.
The peroneus longus is divided at the distal third of the leg, and the proximal end is
sutured to the peroneus brevis.

The peroneus longus is pulled distally and, through a small incision, is weaved through the

The peroneus longus is transferred under the extensor retinaculum to the anterior
compartment.
After placing the foot in neutral or slight dorsiflexion, the tibialis posterior is secured to the
second cuneiform with the use of a biotenodesis screw.
Proximally, tensioning of the tri-tendon anastomosis is done by placing equal tension on
the tibialis anterior and peroneus longus tendons.
Transfer should not be performed until it is determined that the peroneal nerve will not
recover.
Iatrogenic flatfoot is possible after posterior tibial tendon transfer, especially in patients with
preexisting peritalar subluxation.
Options include flexor digitorum longus tendon transfer or talonavicular arthrodesis.
This is an out-of-phase transfer and often behaves as an internal AFO.

Surgical Management
Patients with entrapment or injury to the CPN classically have footdrop with weakness of
the tibialis anterior and EHL tendons and loss of sensation over the anterior ankle and
dorsum of the foot. Motor and sensory symptoms may vary, depending on the location
and extent of nerve injury.
Treatment options depend on the etiology of nerve injury or entrapment and the
severity of symptoms. An AFO with or without dorsiflexion assist should be used to keep
the ankle in a neutral position, to allow for a more normal gait, and to prevent an
equinus contracture. The patient also should undergo physical therapy to help
strengthen weak muscles (important in patients with incomplete symptoms) and to help
maintain flexibility of the ankle to prevent contractures.
In patients with space-occupying lesions, surgical treatment should be performed to
remove the impinging mass and decompress the nerve. Traumatic lacerations of the
CPN should be urgently explored and repaired or reconstructed as appropriate. Nerve

decompression, repair, grafting, and transfers have been described with varying degrees
of success.
In patients with persistent pain and dysfunction and no improvement of symptoms for 9
to 12 months postoperatively, tendon transfers typically are performed. Successful
tendon transfer requires the ankle joint to be supple (passively flexible) and the
transferred tendon to have 5/5 strength; the transferred tendon will lose approximately
one grade of strength (especially if the tendon is out of phase). The most commonly
transferred tendon is the posterior tibial tendon. Lengthening of the Achilles tendon
typically is performed to improve ankle dorsiflexion.
Many types of posterior tibial tendon transfers have been described. Watkins et al30
described a transfer of the posterior tibial tendon through the interosseus membrane
with insertion into the cuneiform or cuboid bone, which resulted in good or excellent
outcomes in 24 of 25 patients. Although this procedure restored the dorsiflexion force of
the ankle, it did not allow for control of varus or valgus positioning of the hindfoot.
McCall et al31 described an alternative procedure, the Bridle procedure, in which a tri-
tendon anastomosis is created proximal to the extensor retinaculum between the
anteriorly transferred posterior tibial tendon, the subcutaneous transfer of the distal
stump of the peroneal longus tendon, and the tibialis anterior tendon. Modification has
since been described that transfers the posterior tibial tendon through the tibialis
anterior tendon and into the middle cuneiform. After the posterior tibial tendon is
secured, the peroneal longus and tibialis anterior tendons are tensioned until
appropriate alignment is achieved and then secured.32
Transfers of the posterior tibial tendon are associated with good to excellent results in
75% to 100% of patients.30-34 Although the procedure does not restore normal
dorsiflexion strength and ankle range of motion, it improves gait and, in most patients,
eliminates the need for a brace or AFO.
